image_description: The image displays three mallard ducks on a wet, paved surface. The primary subject is a male mallard (drake) in the foreground right, standing and facing left, exhibiting characteristic breeding plumage with an iridescent green head, white neck ring, chestnut breast, and grey body. A second drake is in the immediate foreground left, preening its back feathers, showing its side profile and orange webbed feet. A female mallard (hen) with mottled brown plumage is visible in the background, swimming or resting on the wet ground.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Most distinctive feature is the broad, flat bill adapted for filter-feeding; bill is dark grey to yellow-green.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The main drake clearly displays a broad, flat, yellow-green bill typical of mallards. The preening drake's bill is obscured but consistent with the species.
The eye of the main drake is visible and appears dark/black, consistent with the taxonomy.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Body is stocky and compact, streamlined and buoyant with dense waterproof plumage.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The bodies of all three ducks appear robust and compact. The plumage looks dense and well-defined, not matted or unnatural.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Breeding plumage is typically more colorful than female: common patterns include iridescent green head with white neck ring and grey body (mallard), or chestnut head with grey body.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The two male ducks exhibit the classic mallard breeding plumage: iridescent green heads, distinct white neck rings, chestnut breasts, and grey flanks. The female in the background shows the expected mottled brown camouflage pattern.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Legs are short and set far back on the body with webbed feet (three forward toes connected by webbing).
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The orange legs of the standing drakes are visible. They are short and positioned posteriorly. The webbing between the toes is clearly resolved and anatomically correct on the standing drake in the foreground.
The folded wings on the side of the preening drake show the correct layered feather structure and shape. The wing speculum (blue/purple patch with white borders) is visible and correctly placed.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Tail is short with curled central tail feathers (drake feathers) in many species.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The preening drake in the foreground clearly displays the characteristic upward curl of the central tail feathers (drake feathers). The standing drake's tail is less visible but consistent.

selected_experts.reason: To confirm the specific species identification (Mallard) and distinguish it from similar duck species or AI hallucinations.
To verify the structural integrity of the legs and feet, ensuring no fusion or extra limbs, which are common AI artifacts in waterfowl.
To check for edge bleeding between the complex feather layers of the wing and body, and to ensure the head/neck geometry is continuous during the preening pose.
To assess overall texture consistency of the feathers and the wet pavement, looking for subtle smearing or noise patterns.

focus_areas: Webbed foot anatomy and toe separation
Feather texture consistency and edge sharpness
Neck ring continuity and color transition
Bill shape and connection to head

Also, verify that the 'curled tail feathers' on the preening drake are structurally attached and not floating artifacts. Check for any 'melting' where the neck meets the body in the standing drake due to the angle.
